title: Senior's toolkit: the type checker
summary: Run tsc the way CI does, turn on the strict flags that catch real bugs, and read the error codes you will see every day.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: the type checker
steps.body: Types only help if something checks them. In a real repository that is `tsc` with a strict `tsconfig.json`, run in the editor, before you push and in CI. These are the settings and habits that make it catch bugs instead of just making noise.

toolkit.what: Type-check the whole project with its `tsconfig.json` and write nothing. This is the command CI runs; your editor shows the same errors one file at a time.
flags: check only; the bundler or Node produces the JavaScript
use the tsconfig.json in this folder (or give a path)
toolkit.when: before every push; add it as `"typecheck"` in package.json scripts

toolkit.what: One switch in tsconfig.json for the checks that matter: `strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitAny`, `strictFunctionTypes` and more. Every new project should start with it on.
flags: `null` and `undefined` are not silently allowed everywhere
an untyped parameter is an error, not a hidden `any`
`catch (e)` gives `unknown`, so you check it before use

toolkit.what: Not part of `strict`, but many teams turn it on: `arr[i]` and `record[key]` have type `T | undefined`, because the element may not be there.
flags: `name?: string` means "absent", and explicitly passing `undefined` is an error

toolkit.what: Check that a value fits a type without widening it. With `: Type` you lose the precise type of each property; with `satisfies` you keep it and still get the check.
flags: checked against T, x keeps its own, narrower type
toolkit.example: const routes = { home: "/", cart: "/cart" } satisfies Record<string, `/${string}`>;

toolkit.what: Suppress the error on the next line, and report an error (TS2578) if there is none. Use it in tests of invalid input; it never silently outlives the bug it was for.
flags: fails when the error disappears, so stale suppressions get removed
toolkit.example:
// @ts-expect-error: the API must reject a missing id
createOrder({});

toolkit.what: Read the code and the last line first. The four you will see every week:
flags: Type 'X' is not assignable to type 'Y' (an assignment or return)
Argument of type 'X' is not assignable to parameter of type 'Y' (a call)
Property 'p' does not exist on type 'T' (typo, or the union is not narrowed)
toolkit.example: src/cart.ts:14:7 - error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.

steps.prompt: Match each error code to the code that causes it.
pairs: an `@ts-expect-error` above a line that has no error

steps.prompt: After the team turns on `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, CI fails with this. What is the right fix?
options: Handle the empty case: `if (!first) return;` before using it (or `rows.at(0)?.total`)
Turn the flag off again in tsconfig.json
steps.explain: The flag found a real bug: an empty report would crash with `Cannot read properties of undefined`. The non-null assertion `!` and `@ts-ignore` only hide it. Deal with the missing case once, and the type narrows for the rest of the function.

steps.prompt: `satisfies` checks the object but keeps each property's own type. What does this print?
code: const config = { port: 8080, host: "localhost" } satisfies Record<string, string | number>;
steps.explain: Types do not change run-time values: Node strips `satisfies` and runs plain JavaScript. The win is in the editor: with `satisfies`, `config.port` is known to be a `number`, so `config.port + 1` type-checks. With `: Record<string, string | number>` it would be `string | number`.

steps.prompt: Which tsconfig setting makes the compiler catch this bug?
items: A parameter with no type quietly becomes `any`
`items[5].price` on an array that may be shorter
Passing `{ nickname: undefined }` where `nickname?: string` means "leave it out"

steps.prompt: Complete the package.json script CI runs to check types without producing files.
steps.explain: `-p` takes the folder (or file) of the tsconfig.json. `--watch` is for your terminal, never for CI: it never exits.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Start every project with `strict` (and usually `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`) on, and run `tsc --noEmit` in CI so nobody can merge a type error. When you meet an error, read its code and last line, then fix the cause; `!`, `as` and `@ts-ignore` are review questions, not fixes.
